segments.text: But we can think of active inference as being a kind of generalization of reinforcement learning where agents interact with their environment and try to solve a certain task or try to navigate in their environment, but instead of
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: maximizing some utility function or instead of their goal being always maximizing for reward, active inference agents are perhaps more general where the kind of utility function or the general function of active inference agents is always uncertainty minimization.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So active inference agents form some kind of internal model of their environment and they can learn more about their environment by engaging with it through action and then
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: observing what kind of sensory input goes from the environment to the agents.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So there's a kind of duality between perception and action that's always mediated through uncertainty minimization.

segments.text: And because of its generality, this framework can be applied to pretty much any system that's
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: salient enough to persist through time, which was kind of the motivation for the first project, which Alex will talk about a bit more, so I'm only going to mention it briefly, which is the Active Entity Ontology for Science, which really stands at the intersection of three fields, namely DeSci, systems engineering, and active inference, where our aim was to create an
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: ontology that individuals and communities within DeSci can use to collectively minimize their uncertainty about what kind of system they find themselves in and how that system might evolve through time.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And I think this is the same can be done for decentralized AI, which has a lot of similar artifacts that have to do with Web3 and
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: perhaps we can say that either DeSci is encapsulated within decentralized AI or the other way around, depending on which you think is the bigger set.

segments.text: But the core utility of having
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: have a better understanding of the dynamics of our system and be able to better make decisions about what kind of protocols we should create or how should our community interact with other communities and
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: and so on.

segments.text: the open source framework, CatCat, which was developed by Block Science.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And that's been used mainly for token engineering and also just generalized dynamical systems modeling, where you usually take a kind of structural top-down approach to modeling your system of interest, where you define your state space and then you perform giant parameter sweeps to
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: try to figure out how your state space evolves through time and what kind of edge cases can you get to and combining that with active inference cognitive modeling where you have agents that have kind of emergent properties that through collective interaction form these communities that themselves can be
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: can be cast as agents within some environment.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So you have this bottom-up emergent behavior through agents interacting and trying to minimize their uncertainty, as well as a kind of top-down parameter sweep over all the possible states in your system.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: This might sound a little abstract, but I think
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: it's quite relevant for decentralized AI and mainly for two different reasons.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: One of them is we want to create different communities and protocols for both co-owning or creating AI models or interacting with AI models.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And that's already a quite large state space.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So it would definitely be about AI alignment, which is
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: also a very big question and a big problem in AI where
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: you're basically trying to align uncertainty minimization across different types of agents, as well as different levels of your system where DAOs want to minimize their uncertainty with respect to other DAOs or with respect to some preset goal.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: But individuals within those DAOs also need to minimize their uncertainty based on their own preferences, which may or may not align.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: with those of the higher level system.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And the same can be said of AI models and autonomous agents, which are definitely becoming more present in the digital space.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So that would be a very brief overview of some of the projects that we're developing at the Active Inference Institute.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And if you have any questions, then I'm not sure whether we have the time, but thanks a lot for your attention.
